claims.text: The initial material is an FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy feedstock with particle sizes of 15–45 μm.
The baseline deposition uses conventional thermal-spray parameters without additional shielding.
A localized argon or nitrogen shroud can envelop the thermal-spray plume during deposition.
The inert-gas shroud will reduce the in-flight oxidation of FeCoNiCrAl particles.
Reducing particle exposure to ambient oxygen preserves particle-surface integrity.
Preserved particle surfaces exhibit better wettability upon impact.
Preserved particle surfaces promote better bonding upon impact.
A controlled inert-gas flow suppresses the oxidation kinetics of molten or semi-molten particles.
Reduced oxidation improves inter-splat adhesion.
Improved inter-splat adhesion enhances layer accumulation.
Enhanced layer accumulation allows buildup to the desired coating thickness.
The shrouded process will produce a thicker coating than the unshrouded 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline.
The shrouded deposit will maintain a coherent microstructure.
The shrouded deposit will exhibit minimal as-sprayed oxide formation.
Improved particle bonding will make the bond coat more reliable during subsequent high-temperature service in a thermal-barrier-coating system.
The baseline coating has poor deposition efficiency because oxidation degrades splats.
Oxidation-related splat degradation causes the baseline coating to fall short of the required thickness.
The intervention remains effective only if the shroud fully envelops the plume in the critical region before particle impact.
Excessively high deposition rates may diminish the shroud's benefits.
Ambient-gas intrusion may diminish the shroud's benefits.

contradictions.description: The 15–45 μm value is introduced as the feedstock particle-size range, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule treat it as a baseline coating-thickness range. Particle size and deposited coating thickness are different quantities.
